body.text: Human rights commission dealing with record sexual harassment complaints
In short:
New figures reveal a record number of Australians are making workplace sexual harassment complaints, but many are waiting months for cases to be investigated.
The rise is likely due to recent legal reforms and greater awareness of workplace rights, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
What's next?
There is concern the system cannot keep up with the rise in demand, and more money and expertise are needed to handle cases effectively.
More Australians than ever are lodging workplace sexual harassment complaints.
But behind that rise sits an increasingly urgent challenge: adapting the system so it can respond quickly enough to make a difference.
In 2024, at the age of 19, Heather* thought she had secured her dream career after landing an electrical apprenticeship with a small business in New South Wales.
"I was really thinking about the future and trying to set myself up to buy a house," Heather said.
"I felt it was a stable job that would see me through my life."
But those plans were derailed after Heather said she was sexually harassed by her boss, who she alleged made unwelcome advances, while working away.
Traumatised, she quit the apprenticeship the next day.
Supported by the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), Heather lodged a formal complaint with the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC).
It took 14 months for her complaint to be formally accepted for investigation and she was only recently assigned a case manager.
"I feel really trapped in the situation,"
"You feel helpless, like it's never going to happen."
Unable to return to an electrical trade, Heather lost nine months of work before eventually finding a new apprenticeship operating heavy machinery.
Her mother, Melissa Unwin, said the lengthy wait has made it difficult for her daughter to move forward, describing the uncertainty as corrosive and damaging to morale.
"You can't see the end in sight," she said.
"I was 100 per cent blindsided. I trusted this guy with my daughter."
Heather's claims are yet to be tested by the commission and are contested by the owner of the business.
System under pressure

The AHRC remains the preferred avenue for many serious workplace sexual harassment complaints, despite lengthy delays there and alternative pathways through state anti-discrimination bodies and the Fair Work Commission.

Employment lawyer Lisa Berton said complainants tolerated longer wait times because the federal system provided access to broader claims, stronger enforcement powers and potentially uncapped compensation.
"If I was acting for an applicant, I would still select the AHRC, even with the delays," she said.

New figures obtained by the ABC show the AHRC received a record 759 complaints under the Sex Discrimination Act last financial year — up 21 per cent on the previous year and 51 per cent over five years.
Of the 460 sexual harassment complaints received in that period, 95 per cent were related to employment.
Complainants waited an average of nearly seven months just to be allocated a case officer.

While the commission had a target to finalise 85 per cent of complaints within 12 months, the latest figures show 49 per cent of workplace sexual harassment matters took longer than a year to resolve.
Data obtained by the ABC also revealed significant differences between jurisdictions.
In Victoria, workplace sexual harassment complaints were typically processed within one to two weeks and resolved in about two months.
By contrast, Queensland reported an average wait of 246 days for allocation and 424 days to finalisation, while in South Australia, complaints were generally allocated within a week.
NSW reported comparatively short delays, with just 84 complaints awaiting allocation and 98 per cent resolved within a year.
The Fair Work Commission received 183 workplace sexual harassment applications in 2024-25.

Monash University discrimination law professor Dominique Allen said the rise in complaints could reflect greater awareness of workplace rights and confidence in reporting, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
However, Professor Allen said the figures suggested complaint demand was growing faster than the system's capacity to process cases.
"We need more money and expertise put into this so that these claims can be handled more effectively," she said.
The federal government said it had invested $49.8 million in the AHRC since 2022 and would examine the system as part of the upcoming Respect@Work review.
The ETU argued the delays pointed to a deeper problem than growing demand.
The union's NSW/ACT state secretary Allen Hicks said stronger workplace protections only worked if the agencies responsible for enforcing them had enough resources.
"You can have the best laws in the world and if you don't resource the regulatory bodies … then the laws are meaningless," he said.
Unions warn workers walking away
Mr Hicks said the union currently had six members who have been waiting over a year for their AHRC cases to be picked up.
"Young 16 and 17-year-old apprentices who have the courage to stand up and make a formal complaint are put in limbo," Mr Hicks said.
"In construction, witnesses move across six or seven different job sites over 18 months, making it extremely difficult to keep cases together."

Mr Hicks said complaint discontinuance rates at the commission have jumped from 40 per cent to 58 per cent, and a national audit report released in 2025 pointed to delays directly driving workers to give up on their claims.
He said delays threatened broader workforce targets as Australia seeks to add 40,000 more electricians by 2030.
"Stories like this set back female participation by years," he said.
*Heather has been identified by her first name only because of the sensitive nature of the allegations and the ongoing complaints process.
